title: The Rule of Saint Benedict
text:
In the early sixth century, Benedict of Nursia, an Italian who had once lived as a hermit, founded a monastery at Monte Cassino, south of Rome. Around 530 to 540 he wrote a short rule, in 73 chapters, to govern the daily life of his monks. He called it "a little rule for beginners."

The Rule set out a balanced day of communal prayer, manual work and reading. It limited food and drink to moderate portions, allowed for the sick, the old and the very young, and asked the abbot to adapt demands to the strength of each monk. The abbot, elected by the community, held real authority, but was to act like a father and would answer to God for every soul in his care.

One chapter tells the abbot to call the whole community together for any important decision and to hear everyone's advice. Benedict explains that all should be called because God often reveals what is better to the youngest. The abbot then decides, but only after listening.

The Rule spread across Western Europe and, after Charlemagne's time, became the standard rule for most monasteries there. For centuries Benedictine communities preserved books, cleared land, ran schools and kept learning alive. Benedictine monks and nuns still live by the same rule today, nearly fifteen hundred years after it was written.
lesson: A community lasts when its rules are clear, moderate and humane. Ask everyone for their view before big decisions, including the youngest.
source: The Rule of Saint Benedict, especially chapters 2, 3 and 48; Gregory the Great, Dialogues, book 2
